Okay, I’ve kicked off the training script in the background with a 70‑second timeout, redirecting all stdout and stderr into `/tmp/train60.log`. The command is still running (the background job ID is `bz1s7c8r0`), so the log file is being actively appended to. My earlier attempt to read the output directly ran into pipe buffering issues, so I need a more reliable way to inspect what’s been written so far.

What information do I actually need right now? Primarily I want to see the most recent log lines to confirm that training is making progress, and also get a quick sense of how many lines have been written so far (as a proxy for how many logging intervals have passed). Since the training script may be outputting carriage‑return characters (`\r`) to update a progress bar on the same line, I should translate those to newlines first; otherwise `tail` could give me a garbled view. A simple `tr '\r' '\n'` will do that.

I could just `tail -5 /tmp/train60.log`, but that would still include any stray `\r` characters. So I’ll pipe the file through `tr '\r' '\n'` before tailing. That gives me a clean view of the last five logical lines.

Next, to count the total number of lines written, `grep -c "" /tmp/train60.log` is a quick way (it matches every line, including empty ones). This will let me see roughly how many logging steps have occurred.

Putting it together, I need a Bash command that does both operations sequentially: first transform and tail, then count lines. I’ll separate them with a semicolon. The final command will be:

```
tr '\r' '\n' < /tmp/train60.log | tail -5; grep -c "" /tmp/train60.log
```

I’ll invoke this via the Bash tool so I can get the immediate output without waiting for the background process to finish. This should give me a snapshot of the training progress and an indication of how far along the log is.
